records.sourceFile: Consensus on the Use of Therapeutic Interventions in Pain Management, Recovery, and Athletic Performance - A Delphi Study.pdf

paper.citation: McLagan B, Silvey K, Roberts T, Erceg D, Sum JC, Schroeder ET. Consensus on the Use of Therapeutic Interventions in Pain Management, Recovery, and Athletic Performance: A Delphi Study. International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy. 2025;20(3):420-428.
paper.abstract: A four-round Delphi survey of physical therapists and athletic trainers asked when they would consider using percussive, vibration, infrared, heat and cryotherapy. Several local heat, cryotherapy, vibration and percussive uses reached the 70% consideration threshold, but the paper reports no outcome data.
paper.tldr: Clinicians in this survey would consider local heat, vibration or percussive therapy before activity and local cryotherapy for acute joint or soft tissue pain, along with several chronic-pain uses. These are opinions about when to consider a modality, not evidence that it improves recovery or pain.
paper.methods: Delphi survey in four rounds, with experts helping write items and screening criteria requiring licensure, at least 1,000 hours with athletic populations and recent use of one modality. Consensus was set at more than 70% agreement, and 'consideration' meant selecting 'in some instances' or 'in most instances'.
paper.findings: In round 4 (n=32), consideration reached the 70% threshold for local heat (96.9%), local vibration (75.0%) and percussive therapy (75.0%) before activity; local cryotherapy in recovery (93.8%); local cryotherapy for acute joint pain (100%) and acute soft tissue pain (96.9%); local heat (100%) and local cryotherapy (87.5%) for chronic joint pain; and local vibration (84.4%), percussive therapy (78.1%), local heat (100%) and local cryotherapy (87.5%) for chronic soft tissue pain. Local infrared therapy did not reach the threshold in any circumstance, and 81.3% agreed percussive therapy applied directly to the joint should rarely be used for acute joint pain.
paper.limitations: Only 32 of 74 round-1 respondents completed round 4, and the round-4 sample was mostly white and male (29 of 32 men). The authors report that no single response category reached 70% agreement, so they pooled 'In Some Instances' and 'In Most Instances' into a broad 'consideration' measure that cannot rank priorities; Table 1 also omits the consensus asterisk on the 96.9% cryotherapy cell for acute soft tissue pain. The conclusion lists percussive and vibration therapy for recovery, but Table 1 shows 68.8% for both, below the threshold.
paper.practicalImplications: In the listed circumstances, clinicians in this survey would consider local heat before activity, local cryotherapy for acute pain, and heat or cryotherapy for chronic joint pain. Use should still depend on patient presentation, contraindications and available equipment, since the paper finds the choice relies on those factors. Staff should not read these figures as proof that a modality improves outcomes.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff can use these results to see which modalities clinicians would consider before activity, such as local heat or percussive and vibration devices. The data reflect clinician opinion and do not show a performance benefit.
paper.rtp: This paper cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It gives no outcomes, timing or clearance criteria, so its consideration percentages should not be used to set return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Cool water immersion reduces postexercise quadriceps femoris muscle perfusion more than cold water immersion.pdf

paper.citation: Mawhinney C, Heinonen I, Low DA, Han C, Jones H, Kalliokoski KK, et al. Cool-Water Immersion Reduces Postexercise Quadriceps Femoris Muscle Perfusion More Than Cold-Water Immersion. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2022;54(7):1085-1094.
paper.abstract: Healthy men cycled to a core temperature of 38°C and then received 10 minutes of 8°C or 22°C water immersion, or seated rest. Oxygen-15 labeled water PET measured quadriceps muscle perfusion, with cutaneous blood flow and temperature also assessed.
paper.tldr: Ten minutes of 22°C water after cycling reduced global quadriceps blood flow beyond a clinically relevant threshold, while 8°C water did not. Blood flow was measured only for 10 minutes after immersion, so the study does not show a recovery benefit.
paper.methods: Randomized, parallel-group laboratory trial. Thirty recreationally active healthy men were allocated by covariate adaptive randomization (10 per group) and cycled at 70% VO2peak to a core temperature of 38°C, then received 10 minutes of 8°C or 22°C water immersion or seated rest. Quadriceps perfusion was measured by PET with oxygen-15 labeled water, with the post-immersion scan starting 10 minutes after immersion, with skin blood flow by laser Doppler and muscle temperature by needle thermistor.
paper.findings: Global quadriceps perfusion fell by 2.5 mL per 100 g per minute (95% CI -3.9 to -1.1) in 22°C water versus control, above the predefined threshold of 0.75; the 8°C effect on global perfusion was not clinically relevant. Within the quadriceps, 8°C water reduced rectus femoris and vastus lateralis perfusion versus control, and 22°C water reduced vastus lateralis perfusion, while vastus intermedius and vastus medialis were not clinically affected. Thigh skin blood flow fell by 69.3% after 8°C and 52.1% after 22°C, each versus control, and 8°C also reduced calf skin blood flow.
paper.limitations: Ten men per group, with a between-group design and measurements taken only 10 minutes after immersion, so later effects are unknown. Despite matching, the control group had lower VO2peak (41.9 vs 51.1 and 49.7 mL/kg/min) and higher body fat than the cooling groups, no multiplicity adjustment was made, and deep muscle shivering was not measured. Participants were recreationally active men rather than trained athletes, and no women were included.
paper.practicalImplications: When cold-water immersion is used after exercise, staff should know that water temperature changed quadriceps blood flow and muscle temperature in different ways. In this study 22°C water reduced quadriceps blood flow beyond the threshold, while 8°C did not, but the authors do not show a recovery benefit, so this finding alone should not set the water temperature for recovery.
paper.athleteDev: The study measured blood flow and temperature, not performance. It does not show that either water temperature improves or impairs later performance, so it should not inform performance decisions on its own.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It used healthy men after a standardized cycling bout, with no injured muscle, rehabilitation or return-to-play outcome.

records.sourceFile: Dim light sleep tight and wake up bright Sleep optimization in athletes by means of light regulation.pdf

paper.citation: Knufinke M, Nieuwenhuys A, Geurts SAE, Møst EIS, Moen MH, Maase K, et al. Dim light, sleep tight, and wake up bright: Sleep optimization in athletes by means of light regulation. Eur J Sport Sci. 2021;21(1):7-15.
paper.abstract: This crossover study tested whether morning bright light and evening blue-light restriction, combined with fixed sleep-wake times, improve sleep in recreational athletes. Self-reported sleep onset latency improved, with larger effects in athletes who kept strict schedules, but actigraphy showed no differences. Adherence to the fixed sleep-wake schedule was low, and the light-emitting goggles were rated rather uncomfortable.
paper.tldr: Morning bright light and evening amber glasses shortened self-reported sleep onset in recreational athletes by 8 to 17 minutes, depending on schedule adherence. Objective sleep did not change, and the goggles were uncomfortable, so less obtrusive methods are needed.
paper.methods: Within-subject crossover with counterbalanced order. Athletes completed a light-regulation week and a control week, with a standardized bed and rise time (maximum deviation 30 minutes) and guidance on caffeine and alcohol. Sleep was measured with diaries and wrist actigraphy, and effects were analyzed with repeated-measures ANOVA in two datasets: 8 athletes with strict schedules and 25 with more variable schedules.
paper.findings: Self-reported sleep onset latency was 17 minutes shorter with light regulation in the strict dataset (F(1,7) = 14.64, p = .006) and 8 minutes shorter in the 25-athlete dataset (p = .023). Subjective sleep quality improved in the strict dataset (by 0.42 on a 10-point scale, p = .011) but not in the larger dataset. No actigraphy-based sleep measure differed significantly between conditions, and lights-off time in the larger dataset was about 27 minutes later with light regulation.
paper.limitations: Only 8 athletes met the strict schedule criteria, and the two datasets were built after low schedule adherence was found. Athletes who adhered may have believed in the intervention, and sleep ratings were taken on waking, when sleep inertia may affect them. Morning and evening components were combined, so their separate effects cannot be judged, and the authors note light exposure was not consistently timed.
paper.practicalImplications: Morning bright light with evening blue-light restriction may shorten self-reported sleep onset in recreational athletes who keep fairly regular schedules. The light-emitting goggles were rated rather uncomfortable and athletes had difficulty wearing the evening glasses for the full three hours, so plan for practical barriers. The stronger effects came from athletes who kept fixed bed and rise times, so schedule regularity should come first.
paper.athleteDev: For sleep as part of recovery planning, light regulation may help athletes who keep regular bed and rise times, with self-reported onset up to 17 minutes faster. The authors suggest combining it with other sleep hygiene measures rather than using it alone, and objective sleep did not change.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested recreational athletes without severe sleep complaints and did not assess injured athletes, recovery from injury or readiness to return to competition.

records.sourceFile: Does wet-cupping therapy improve repeated sprint ability, perceived wellness, and rating of perceived exertion in young active males.pdf

paper.citation: Dergaa I, Ghram A, Romdhani M, Souissi A, Ammar A, Farahat RA, et al. Does wet-cupping therapy improve repeated sprint ability, perceived wellness, and rating of perceived exertion in young active males? Sports Med Health Sci. 2023.
paper.abstract: In 49 active men, repeated sprint performance, wellness and perceived exertion were compared between a control session and a session 24 hours after wet-cupping therapy. Sprint power was higher, and perceived sleep, stress and exertion were lower, after cupping.
paper.tldr: Wet-cupping 24 hours before testing was followed by higher sprint power and lower perceived exertion and stress in this single-group study. Because there was no sham comparator, the results should be treated as preliminary.
paper.methods: Single-group experimental design with a control session and a post-cupping session two weeks apart, in counterbalanced order, in 49 active adult men. Wet-cupping (250-300 mmHg, superficial scarification) was applied 24 hours before testing. Outcomes were a six-sprint running test (maximum, mean and minimum power), the Hooper wellness questionnaire and Foster CR-10 RPE. Paired t-tests and effect sizes were used.
paper.findings: In Table 1, maximum, mean and minimum sprint power were higher after cupping than in the control session (mean differences 68.64 W, 43.32 W and 30.76 W; all p = 0.001; effect sizes 0.6, 0.6 and 0.5). Perceived sleep (mean difference 0.97, effect size 0.9), perceived stress (0.46, effect size 0.6) and RPE (0.71, effect size 1.1) were better after cupping. Perceived fatigue and muscle soreness did not differ (p = 0.26 and 0.79).
paper.limitations: Single-arm design without a sham or blinded comparison, and a single post-treatment session. Participants were police officers rather than athletes and were not in a fatiguing training block, so the fatigue and soreness results may not generalize. Nitric oxide, lactate and other mechanistic markers were not measured. The abstract gives p < 0.05 (maximum power) and p < 0.01 (mean and minimum power), mean power ES 0.5, minimum power ES 0.6 and sleep ES 0.85, while Table 1 gives p = 0.001 for all three, mean power ES 0.6, minimum power ES 0.5 and sleep ES 0.9.
paper.practicalImplications: Cupping is not established as a performance aid by this study. Staff should not add it to sprint preparation on the strength of these results, and any use should follow safety and hygiene standards, because the authors note risks of scarring, bruising and infection.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: this study does not support using wet-cupping to improve sprint performance or reduce exertion. The reported gains come from a single-group design with no sham comparator and need to be replicated in controlled trials before any performance recommendation.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It tested healthy men without injury, and it did not assess muscle damage, soreness or readiness after injury or illness.

records.sourceFile: Dose-response relationship between evening exercise and sleep.pdf

paper.citation: Leota J, Presby DM, Le F, Czeisler ME, Mascaro L, Capodilupo ER, et al. Dose-response relationship between evening exercise and sleep. Nature Communications. 2025;16:3297.
paper.abstract: In 14,689 physically active adults wearing a wrist biometric device for one year (4,084,354 person-nights), later exercise timing and higher exercise strain were associated with delayed sleep onset, shorter sleep, lower sleep quality, higher nocturnal resting heart rate and lower nocturnal heart rate variability. Exercise ending at least 4 hours before sleep onset was not associated with changes in sleep, regardless of strain.
paper.tldr: In physically active adults, hard exercise late in the evening was linked to later sleep onset, shorter sleep, and higher overnight resting heart rate with lower HRV. The authors suggest finishing exercise at least 4 hours before sleep onset, or choosing lighter sessions if evening training cannot move earlier.
paper.methods: Retrospective cohort using WHOOP wearable data from September 2021 to August 2022, including adults with at least 350 days of wear and at least 50 logged exercises in the analysis window. Exercise timing was measured relative to each participant's habitual sleep onset and to actual sleep onset that night, and strain was the summated heart rate zone score grouped into light, moderate, high and maximal. Generalized additive mixed models with a random intercept for participant were used, with contrasts at 2-hour intervals and p < 0.005.
paper.findings: Maximal rather than light strain ending 2 hours before habitual sleep onset was associated with 36.0 minutes later sleep onset, 22.2 minutes less sleep, 0.87 percentage points lower sleep quality, 3.9 bpm higher nocturnal RHR and 8.3 RMSSD units (14.1%) lower. Ending 2 hours after habitual sleep onset produced larger differences (80.0 minutes later onset, 42.6 minutes less sleep, 5.6 percentage points lower quality, 9.4 bpm higher RHR and 14.6 RMSSD units (32.6%) lower). When light or moderate strain ended more than about 2 hours before habitual sleep onset, sleep onset and sleep quality were similar to non-exercise nights.
paper.limitations: The design is observational, so the associations cannot show that exercise caused the changes, and light exposure, caffeine, alcohol and diet were not controlled. Sleep onset was detected by the device rather than by sleep attempt, and the strain score (SHRZS) may underestimate strength training. The sample was physically active adults rather than athletes, 73.8% men, and two authors are WHOOP employees whose employer provided salaries.
paper.practicalImplications: For physically active adults, finishing hard or long sessions at least 4 hours before habitual sleep onset is the timing the data support for protecting sleep. If evening training cannot move earlier, lighter sessions in that window were associated with smaller sleep and heart rate changes than maximal sessions.
paper.athleteDev: Use the timing rule to place the last high-strain session of the day, since later and harder sessions were linked to delayed and shorter sleep. The authors' comment on evening elite competitions is discussion, not a measured result, because the sample was not athletes and sport performance was not measured.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions because it included no injured athletes and did not link sleep or heart rate measures to injury, symptoms or clearance.
